source_read: PMC HTML full text PMC8956974 (JAMA Netw Open 2022;5(3):e223849): Key Points, abstract, all sections, Tables 1 and 2 as text, and the article notes (author contributions, conflict-of-interest disclosures, funding). Figures 1-3 print no values; I viewed them enlarged on the PMC figure pages in my own tab and read them only approximately. Also read the correction notice PMC9021906 (JAMA Netw Open 2022;5(4):e2212024), which rewords the abstract's first Conclusions sentence; the PMC article text still shows the uncorrected sentence. The supplement (PDF) was not read.

claims.overstatement: Incomplete rather than overstated. The claim says the lower hypertension risk of moderate drinkers was no longer statistically clear after six lifestyle factors (right), but omits that at light intake (more than 0 to 8.4 drinks a week) the adjusted hazard ratio stays below 1 (about 0.90, with an interval excluding 1, read approximately from Figure 1A). The cohorts claim includes this qualification for coronary disease; this claim should too. Reference group: 'people who did not drink' is the source's abstainers group (0 drinks a week at baseline); the main text does not say whether former drinkers were excluded, and the claim could say so.
claims.note: Numbers check: OR 1.28 (1.18 to 1.39) per 1-SD increase in genetically predicted consumption (AUD-Restricted score, inverse-variance weighted; disease associations tested in current drinkers, per the Table 2 footnote). Allele score per 1 drink/day: light 1.3 (1.1 to 1.5), moderate 1.7 (1.3 to 2.2), highest category (>24.5 drinks/week) 2.6 (1.6 to 4.2). The six lifestyle factors match the Methods. Unit caveat: the Methods say each instrument was standardized to a 1 drink/day difference, while Table 2 reports per 1-SD; the SD is never defined. Instrument: F 780. Pathway checks: variants associated with eight risk factors were removed; 34 423 lifelong abstainers served as a negative control for continuous traits (pleiotropy signal for HDL and apolipoprotein A only); MR-Egger intercepts were not significant.

anchors.locator: Table 2, hypertension row and footnote; Results › Traditional MR, 2nd paragraph
anchors.extracted: IVW, AUD-Restricted score: hypertension OR 1.28 (1.18 to 1.39; P=1.73x10^-9) per 1-SD genetically predicted consumption, tested in current drinkers; threshold P<.008; weighted median, MR-Egger, MR-PRESSO and excluding abstainers said to support it (eTables).

Allele score per 1 drink/day within drinking categories, hypertension: light 1.3 (1.1 to 1.5; P=.003), moderate 1.7 (1.3 to 2.2; P<.001), highest 2.6 (1.6 to 4.2); male light drinkers 1.4 (1.1 to 1.8).

anchors.locator: Results › Traditional MR, 1st paragraph; Results › Evaluating Association Shapes, 2nd paragraph; Figure 3C-D
anchors.extracted: Genetically predicted intake associated with higher systolic and diastolic pressure (values in eTable 7, not read); quadratic nonlinear fits for systolic (P<.001) and diastolic (P=.001) pressure; curves plotted only, roughly +12 mm Hg systolic at 21 drinks/week.

anchors.locator: Results › Observational Associations With Cardiovascular Diseases and Lifestyle Factors, 1st paragraph; Figure 1A; Methods › Statistical Analysis, 1st paragraph
anchors.extracted: Against abstainers (0 drinks/week), moderate intake (>8.4 to 15.4 US drinks of 14 g/week) had a significantly lower hypertension hazard at baseline, not significant after six lifestyle factors. Figure 1A, approximate: light about 0.78 baseline, 0.90 adjusted (interval below 1); moderate about 0.86, then 1.00.

claims.note: The UK Biobank sentence matches the source. The six factors are as listed in the Methods. Moderate intake (>8.4 to 15.4 US drinks of 14 g a week) lost statistical significance after adjustment. Figure 1B prints no values; read approximately, coronary artery disease at light intake was about 0.76 at baseline and 0.86 adjusted, with an interval below 1; at moderate intake about 0.87, then 0.96, with an interval including 1. So 'reduced but did not remove it at light intake' is right as an approximate reading. The reference group is abstainers at 0 drinks/week at baseline; whether former drinkers were excluded is only in eMethods 3 (not read). The authors' suggestion that unmeasured factors might remove the light-drinking association is speculation (Discussion, 2nd paragraph).

anchors.locator: Results › Observational Associations With Cardiovascular Diseases and Lifestyle Factors, 1st paragraph; Figure 1B
anchors.extracted: J- or U-shaped associations for all six diseases; light and moderate drinkers healthier (less smoking, lower BMI, more activity and vegetables, better self-rated health); moderate-intake CAD hazard significant at baseline, not after six lifestyle factors. Figure 1B approximate: light 0.76 then 0.86 (below 1); moderate 0.87 then 0.96.

Cox models against abstainers (0 drinks/week); light >0-8.4, moderate >8.4-15.4, heavy >15.4-24.5, highest >24.5 US drinks of 14 g a week; adjusted for smoking, BMI, physical activity, cooked vegetable and red meat intake, self-reported health.
Authors suggest that unmeasured or unknown factors may further attenuate, or remove, the residual lower risk among light drinkers; untested.

claims.overstatement: Three wording points. (1) 'whose key assumption was not tested': the main text does not report a test of whether the score shifts intake equally at every level of drinking, but the supplement (eMethods 10, not read) might; write 'not reported as tested in the main text'. (2) '371,463 people' is the full sample; the disease estimates were computed in current drinkers (Table 2 footnote), whose number is not printed. (3) The claim reports the secondary score's threshold and slight decreases, but not that the authors attribute them to residual pleiotropy in that score; a reader should know the authors discount them.
claims.note: Numbers check: CAD 1.38 (1.10 to 1.74; P=.006), MI 1.37 (1.05 to 1.78; P=.02, above P<.008), 5-variant AUD-Restricted score, F 780, quadratic fit P<.001, AUDIT-C-Restricted piecewise threshold roughly 7 to 14 drinks of 14 g a week. 'A unit the paper does not define' is fair: Table 2 is per 1-SD, but the Methods say each score was standardized to 1 drink/day, and the SD is not given. Instrument strength and pathway checks: beta 7.0 drinks/week, F 780; 4 of 9 AUD variants removed for association with eight risk factors; no association with confounders (eTables 4-6, not read); a lifelong-abstainer negative control (continuous traits; HDL and apolipoprotein A pleiotropy); MR-Egger, weighted median and MR-PRESSO consistent; multivariable nonlinear MR adjusted for smoking, BMI and depression. Read approximately, the fitted curves reach implausibly large odds ratios (about 36 for hypertension and 150 for CAD at about 33 drinks/week, against observational hazard ratios near 1.5 and 1.3 at the top category), which weakens confidence in the curve shape.

anchors.locator: Table 2, coronary artery disease and myocardial infarction rows; Methods › Statistical Analysis, 2nd paragraph
anchors.extracted: IVW per 1-SD genetically predicted consumption: CAD 1.38 (1.10 to 1.74; P=6.00x10^-3); MI 1.37 (1.05 to 1.78; P=2.00x10^-2); Bonferroni threshold for six diseases P<.008.

anchors.locator: Methods › Genetic Instruments for Alcohol Consumption; Results › Associations Between Genetic Instruments and Alcohol Intake Phenotypes
anchors.extracted: AUD score (9 variants, published GWAS) reduced to 5 by removing variants tied to smoking, BMI, activity, vegetables, red meat, health rating, CRP or cholesterol; scaled to 1 drink/day; beta 7.0 drinks/week, P<.001, F 780.
In 34 423 lifelong abstainers no association with the continuous traits, and MR-Egger intercepts not significant, except a potential pleiotropic effect on HDL cholesterol and apolipoprotein A.

anchors.locator: Methods › Statistical Analysis, 3rd paragraph; Results › Evaluating Association Shapes, 1st paragraph; Figure 2
anchors.extracted: Nonlinear MR: estimates in deciles of residual intake, fitted by fractional polynomial or piecewise models; no test of a constant genetic effect across strata reported. Quadratic best (P<.001); every amount raised risk. Figure 2 approximate: CAD OR 1.3 at 7, 2.8 at 14, 9 at 21, 150 at 33 drinks/week.

Secondary AUDIT-C-Restricted score: piecewise threshold, no higher risk until roughly 7 to 14 drinks/week; slight decreases at modest intake for hypertension and in some women's analyses, attributed by the authors to residual pleiotropy and low power; not seen with ADH1B alone or after removing abstainers.
Authors concede the associations may reflect a shared genetic basis rather than a causal effect, and that AUD variants are an indirect proxy for usual intake.

claims.note: Stroke OR 1.26 (1.04 to 1.54; P=2.10x10^-2) per 1-SD, which does not meet the paper's P<.008 threshold for six diseases; the claim says so correctly. The authors nonetheless describe the other phenotypes as supporting the primary results. Table 1 counts 8710 strokes in the whole sample; the number analysed (current drinkers) is not printed.

anchors.locator: Table 2, stroke row; Methods › Statistical Analysis, 2nd paragraph
anchors.extracted: IVW, AUD-Restricted score: stroke OR 1.26 (1.04 to 1.54; P=2.10x10^-2) per 1-SD genetically predicted consumption; significance threshold for diseases P<.008.
Text says MR analyses of the other cardiovascular phenotypes supported the primary observations, without noting that stroke, MI and heart failure missed the stated threshold.

claims.overstatement: Minor. The case counts (14,367 atrial fibrillation, 5,812 heart failure) are whole-sample counts from Table 1; the genetic estimates were computed in current drinkers (Table 2 footnote), whose case numbers are not printed. Write 'in a sample with 14,367 cases' or drop the counts.
claims.note: Numbers check: AF 1.24 (1.08 to 1.44; P=3.00x10^-3), significant at P<.008; heart failure 1.39 (1.08 to 1.78; P=9.00x10^-3), not significant at that threshold, as the claim says. The estimates are per 1-SD of genetically predicted consumption, a unit that is not defined. Similar quadratic shapes for other cardiovascular diseases are only in the supplement (eFigure 6).

anchors.locator: Table 2, heart failure and atrial fibrillation rows
anchors.extracted: IVW per 1-SD genetically predicted consumption: heart failure OR 1.39 (1.08 to 1.78; P=9.00x10^-3), atrial fibrillation 1.24 (1.08 to 1.44; P=3.00x10^-3); threshold P<.008; disease tests in current drinkers.
Whole sample of 371 463: heart failure 5812 (1.56%), atrial fibrillation 14 367 (3.87%); counts for the current-drinker analysis are not given.

key_findings.note: My approximate readings of Figure 1 agree (CAD light adjusted about 0.86).

key_findings.correction: In the text, the lifelong-abstainer check (34 423 people) covers the continuous traits discussed in that paragraph (GGT, blood pressure, LDL; HDL and apolipoprotein A showed a pleiotropic signal). No disease results for lifelong abstainers are printed in the main text, although the Table 2 footnote says abstainers were used to test for pleiotropy. Read: 'the score was not associated with the continuous traits in 34 423 lifelong abstainers ...'.

key_findings.note: The female light-drinker CAD result is printed with 'P < .09'.
Approximate readings agree; at about 33 drinks/week the curves reach about 36 (hypertension) and 150 (CAD).
That no disease outcomes were analysed there is consistent with the supplement titles (eTable 14, eFigure 15: blood pressure only).

reporting_issues.note: Found independently: the axes are U/L, mg/dL and mm Hg.

risk_of_bias.note: Overall high, driven by the stratified and nonlinear analyses that carry the headline; I agree that the linear estimates alone would merit some concerns. The confounding note's 'abstainers include former drinkers' is an inference: the main text defines abstainers only as 0 drinks/week.

interpretation_gap.note: Substantial. Also note that the Discussion's remarks about 7 and 14 drinks a week as thresholds rest on the fitted curves; no claim should carry them as amounts.
